RECORDS FORMAT (step records-format): a parser for docs/harness/RULES.md and docs/harness/BACKLOG.md with a fixed pointer grammar. LEDGER pointers name the repo, the run id and the 1-based line number in that run's append-only .jsonl (never a timestamp: 32 of 308 events in the ledgers checker-29 read share one). FILE pointers name the repo, the path, a commit sha and a verbatim anchor string that must occur in that file at that commit (never path:line). ORIGIN pointers mark a want first filed in BACKLOG.md itself, with the date and who filed it. OWNER pointers read 'owner, chat, YYYY-MM-DD' with the owner's words quoted; they are unresolvable by kind and are printed as such. Every RULES entry has an id, a scope (all, or one repo from a fixed list of repos with public remotes), the verbatim text, a source pointer, and the check a checker uses to decide held or failed. A scan rejects absolute paths (drive letters, /c/, /home/, /Users/, /tmp/), IP addresses, e-mail addresses, ssh key file names and every word in the private-names file. Tests run on fixtures only; no content yet.

RECORDS OF RECORD (step records-of-record): RULES.md holds the standing rules the lead retypes into briefs, and the procedures the ledgers show: record a run from a worktree at origin's default branch with a CRLF-insensitive ledger comparison and a checkout restore; rebase only over other runs' ledgers, with a patch-id map; record re-run judgements before a verdict relies on them; live-before and live-after notes; V3 ships only through deploy/install.sh on the owner's word, recorded in the ship note; a correction note when the shared checkout holds another session's commit. docs/HARNESS.md's public-repo rule ('no box details', 'no secrets', 'none of the operator's private writings') is entered as a rule even though tracked content violates it today (docs/RUNBOOK.md names the box host); a checker confirms it as FAILED, so it resets to interval 1 and stays due, and the violation is a want in BACKLOG.md. BACKLOG.md holds every technical want of the lead's private backlog that passes the scan, with a LEDGER or FILE pointer where a public record exists and an ORIGIN pointer where none does. Ideas raised in chat that the owner has not approved for filing stay private. The lead's private backlog marks every item it keeps back as 'awaiting the owner' or 'local-only', so a checker can confirm that every item is either in BACKLOG.md or marked. Tests: ids unique; statuses from a fixed set (open, filed-as-run, done, refused); the scan passes; every pointer into this repo resolves (the anchor occurs at the named commit). tools/context.py check (built in this step, and never subject to the assembly step's refusal) resolves every pointer through the roots file and prints each one that does not resolve; the step's checker runs it on the lead's machine and requires 0 unresolved pointers (OWNER and ORIGIN pointers excepted). ASSEMBLY (step assembly): tools/context.py brief --role builder|checker|lead ROOT RUN [STEP] reads RULES.md and BACKLOG.md, and loads the harness's Ledger class and done_problems, from a named concordance-2 commit through git show, never the working copy: for a step of a run in concordance-2 it is the step's base commit, so no step can change the brief its own checker receives; with no STEP, or for a run in another repo, it is concordance-2's HEAD, which no step of that run can change. The brief prints the sha it used. brief refuses to run when tools/context.py differs from HEAD, so its tests run it inside temporary repositories where it is committed. Sections: CORE (the rules in scope, verbatim, by id, never truncated); IN FLIGHT (every open step in the ledgers of the repos on the fixed public list only, located through the roots file: repo, run, step, owner and state; no paths); RUN (goal, criteria, the step's claim, scope and tests, previous findings; the checker role carries the content of cmd_brief and none of the builder's narrative); WANTS (backlog items for this repo or run, past a size cap as pointers only); DUE (rules due under the schedule). Every line names its pointer; LEDGER and FILE pointers are resolved and any that does not resolve is printed UNRESOLVED, never dropped. Before printing, brief scans its whole output with the private-names words and the harness's secret patterns only, and on a hit refuses, naming the line number and the kind of hit, never the matched word. The path and IP rules are applied only to text brief writes itself; a line it quotes from a ledger that a path or IP rule hits (today's public ledgers quote the box install path and 127.0.0.1 in 4 of 8 runs) is printed as its LEDGER pointer instead of its text. Tests: a fixture plan naming a /home/ path and 127.0.0.1 still yields a brief, with those lines as pointers; an invented private name refuses; a fixture roots file listing an invented private repo with an open step never puts that name in a brief; identical bytes for identical records; the CORE of two different runs of the same scope is byte-identical; the output is unchanged when the entries of RULES.md or BACKLOG.md are reordered or their line endings switch; the cap never shortens CORE; a subprocess no-write test (ignoring .git/index refreshes); refusal on a modified tools/context.py.

SCHEDULE (step schedule): a confirmation is a ledger note of kind confirm, text 'RULE <id> held|failed: <evidence>', by a checker id (checker-N) that has a verdict event in the same ledger; confirmations by the lead, a builder or any other checker are ignored and listed as ignored. THE CLOCK: a run is complete when the harness's own done_problems returns nothing, and it completes at its last passing live verdict; the runs in a rule's scope are numbered 1, 2, 3, ... in the order of those verdicts' timestamps (ties broken by repo name, then run id); a brief assembled at time t is in run n = 1 + the number of runs in scope completed before t; a confirmation is placed by its own timestamp t_c, in run c = 1 + the number of runs in scope completed before t_c, so a confirmation in a run that stalls, is blocked or is superseded never pins the rule; a rule's entry is number 0, at the commit that added it to RULES.md. THE GEAR: a rule at interval index i (starting at 1) whose last counted confirmation is in run c (0 at entry) is DUE in run n when n - c >= F(i+1) (intervals 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...); a held confirmation in a run where it is due sets c = n and i = i + 1; a failed confirmation sets c = n and i = 1 at any time; any other confirmation is recorded and listed but not counted. So an always-held rule confirmed whenever due is confirmed in runs 1, 3, 6, 11, 19, ..., F(m+3)-2. Tests: the interval sequence and the reset; the confirmation runs equal F(m+3)-2 for m up to 10; two held confirmations in one run count once; the schedule is identical when the ledgers are read in a different file order (order within a file is kept); the tie rule; a confirmation inside a run that never completes still lets the rule fall due later; ignored confirmations are listed. Staggered starts, the j-th rule's first due run spread by frac(j*phi) over the first F(k) runs (k the least with F(k) >= the number of rules) are MEASURED against unstaggered starts, assuming every rule always holds and is confirmed whenever due, as the largest number of rules due in any one run over the first 100 runs, and adopted only if they lower it; the step reports both numbers.

goal: A method to ASSEMBLE and REAPPLY context for the harness's own work, at the scope the owner chose on 2026-11-03 ('our working method first'). A fresh builder or checker, a new session, or the lead after a context compaction gets the same working context from RECORDS - tracked files and the harness's append-only ledgers, which may be uncommitted while a run is open - never from narrative memory or a transcript search; every assembled line names the record it came from, so it is re-verified when it is reapplied. A first draft of this method was opened in a ledger and withdrawn before any commit, after checker-29's plan review failed it with 11 findings; this run's first plan answered them and failed with 7 more, its second with 3 more, its third with 3 more, its fourth with 1 more; this plan answers those. The owner named two structures: 'Eigenvectors and Fibonacci gears. Two structures.' EIGENVECTORS: the brief's CORE is the fixed point of reapplication - the standing rules in scope, verbatim, byte-identical every time they are assembled for the same scope (two different runs of one scope get the same CORE), unchanged by restating the inputs (entry order, line endings), never truncated - and the literal eigenvalue does its work in the schedule: Fibonacci intervals grow at the rate phi, the dominant eigenvalue of [[1,1],[1,0]] (eigenvector (phi, 1)), so a rule that keeps holding costs only logarithmically many re-checks. A spectral (eigenvector) ranking of rules is NOT built here: checker-29 showed on a 5-node example that power iteration on an acyclic citation graph reduces to plain counts, and a graph of source pointers is acyclic by construction, since a record can only name a record that existed before it; it is filed as a want, to be measured once checkers' confirmations give a co-confirmation matrix. FIBONACCI GEARS: each rule's re-verification interval steps through 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... runs in its scope; a checker's confirmation made while the rule is due advances it, a failure resets it to 1; an always-held rule confirmed whenever due is confirmed in its runs 1, 3, 6, 11, 19, ..., that is m times in its first F(m+3)-2 runs (8 times in 100). It lives in concordance-2 as a light tool on top of the harness; tools/harness.py, .claude/agents/* and every other grader are not edited. Nothing deploys to the box: the new files are accepted drift, named exactly, until the next concordance-2 deploy.

This run does not push until V3's 2026-11-03-restatement-audit ledger is on origin, because this plan and its fixtures name that run's step and agents.

PRIVATE CONFIGURATION: everything private stays outside the repo, in ~/.config/harness/ beside the existing secret_patterns.txt: a roots file mapping each repo name to its local checkout (used to resolve pointers into sibling repos and to read their ledgers) and a private-names file (the names of repositories without a public remote, and any other words the scan must reject). The directory is found through an explicit override, HARNESS_CONFIG_DIR, when it is set (as HARNESS_SECRET_PATTERNS already overrides the harness's own file), because on Windows Python reads USERPROFILE, so pointing HOME elsewhere does not hide ~/.config/harness; a test proves that with the override set (and HARNESS_SECRET_PATTERNS set, since the harness's secret scan reads that directory too) the real directory is never opened. The tool reads both files when present and works without them; tests use fixture copies with invented names through the override; neither file's content appears in the repo, in any brief, or in any test id (the harness writes failing test ids into the public ledger).

RECORDS FORMAT (step records-format): a parser for docs/harness/RULES.md and docs/harness/BACKLOG.md with a fixed pointer grammar. LEDGER pointers name the repo, the run id and the 1-based line number in that run's append-only .jsonl (never a timestamp: 32 of 308 events in the ledgers checker-29 read share one). FILE pointers name the repo, the path, a commit sha and a verbatim anchor string that must occur in that file at that commit (never path:line). ORIGIN pointers mark a want first filed in BACKLOG.md itself, with the date and who filed it. OWNER pointers read 'owner, chat, YYYY-MM-DD' with the owner's words quoted; they are unresolvable by kind and are printed as such. Every RULES entry has an id, a scope (all, or one repo from a fixed list of repos with public remotes), the verbatim text, a source pointer, and the check a checker uses to decide held or failed. A scan rejects absolute paths (drive letters, /c/, /home/, /Users/, /tmp/), IP addresses, e-mail addresses, ssh key file names and every word in the private-names file. Tests run on fixtures only; no content yet.

RECORDS OF RECORD (step records-of-record): RULES.md holds the standing rules the lead retypes into briefs, and the procedures the ledgers show: record a run from a worktree at origin's default branch with a CRLF-insensitive ledger comparison and a checkout restore; rebase only over other runs' ledgers, with a patch-id map; record re-run judgements before a verdict relies on them; live-before and live-after notes; V3 ships only through deploy/install.sh on the owner's word, recorded in the ship note; a correction note when the shared checkout holds another session's commit. docs/HARNESS.md's public-repo rule ('no box details', 'no secrets', 'none of the operator's private writings') is entered as a rule even though tracked content violates it today (docs/RUNBOOK.md names the box host); a checker confirms it as FAILED, so it resets to interval 1 and stays due, and the violation is a want in BACKLOG.md. BACKLOG.md holds every technical want of the lead's private backlog that passes the scan, with a LEDGER or FILE pointer where a public record exists and an ORIGIN pointer where none does. Ideas raised in chat that the owner has not approved for filing stay private. The lead's private backlog marks every item it keeps back as 'awaiting the owner' or 'local-only', so a checker can confirm that every item is either in BACKLOG.md or marked. Tests: ids unique; statuses from a fixed set (open, filed-as-run, done, refused); the scan passes; every pointer into this repo resolves (the anchor occurs at the named commit). tools/context.py check (built in this step, and never subject to the assembly step's refusal) resolves every pointer through the roots file and prints each one that does not resolve; the step's checker runs it on the lead's machine and requires 0 unresolved pointers (OWNER and ORIGIN pointers excepted). ASSEMBLY (step assembly): tools/context.py brief --role builder|checker|lead ROOT RUN [STEP] reads RULES.md and BACKLOG.md, and loads the harness's Ledger class and done_problems, from a named concordance-2 commit through git show, never the working copy: for a step of a run in concordance-2 it is the step's base commit, so no step can change the brief its own checker receives; with no STEP, or for a run in another repo, it is concordance-2's HEAD, which no step of that run can change. The brief prints the sha it used. brief refuses to run when tools/context.py differs from HEAD, so its tests run it inside temporary repositories where it is committed. Sections: CORE (the rules in scope, verbatim, by id, never truncated); IN FLIGHT (every open step in the ledgers of the repos on the fixed public list only, located through the roots file: repo, run, step, owner and state; no paths); RUN (goal, criteria, the step's claim, scope and tests, previous findings; the checker role carries the content of cmd_brief and none of the builder's narrative); WANTS (backlog items for this repo or run, past a size cap as pointers only); DUE (rules due under the schedule). Every line names its pointer; LEDGER and FILE pointers are resolved and any that does not resolve is printed UNRESOLVED, never dropped. Before printing, brief scans its whole output with the private-names words and the harness's secret patterns only, and on a hit refuses, naming the line number and the kind of hit, never the matched word. The path and IP rules are applied only to text brief writes itself; a line it quotes from a ledger that a path or IP rule hits (today's public ledgers quote the box install path and 127.0.0.1 in 4 of 8 runs) is printed as its LEDGER pointer instead of its text. Tests: a fixture plan naming a /home/ path and 127.0.0.1 still yields a brief, with those lines as pointers; an invented private name refuses; a fixture roots file listing an invented private repo with an open step never puts that name in a brief; identical bytes for identical records; the CORE of two different runs of the same scope is byte-identical; the output is unchanged when the entries of RULES.md or BACKLOG.md are reordered or their line endings switch; the cap never shortens CORE; a subprocess no-write test (ignoring .git/index refreshes); refusal on a modified tools/context.py.

SCHEDULE (step schedule): a confirmation is a ledger note of kind confirm, text 'RULE <id> held|failed: <evidence>', by a checker id (checker-N) that has a verdict event in the same ledger; confirmations by the lead, a builder or any other checker are ignored and listed as ignored. THE CLOCK: a run is complete when the harness's own done_problems returns nothing, and it completes at its last passing live verdict; the runs in a rule's scope are numbered 1, 2, 3, ... in the order of those verdicts' timestamps (ties broken by repo name, then run id); a brief assembled at time t is in run n = 1 + the number of runs in scope completed before t; a confirmation is placed by its own timestamp t_c, in run c = 1 + the number of runs in scope completed before t_c, so a confirmation in a run that stalls, is blocked or is superseded never pins the rule; a rule's entry is number 0, at the commit that added it to RULES.md. THE GEAR: a rule at interval index i (starting at 1) whose last counted confirmation is in run c (0 at entry) is DUE in run n when n - c >= F(i+1) (intervals 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ...); a held confirmation in a run where it is due sets c = n and i = i + 1; a failed confirmation sets c = n and i = 1 at any time; any other confirmation is recorded and listed but not counted. So an always-held rule confirmed whenever due is confirmed in runs 1, 3, 6, 11, 19, ..., F(m+3)-2. Tests: the interval sequence and the reset; the confirmation runs equal F(m+3)-2 for m up to 10; two held confirmations in one run count once; the schedule is identical when the ledgers are read in a different file order (order within a file is kept); the tie rule; a confirmation inside a run that never completes still lets the rule fall due later; ignored confirmations are listed. STAGGERED FIRST CHECKS, AMENDED (step stagger-cap): a rule never yet confirmed must be checked soon, so its first due run is spread by frac(j*phi) over at most the first 13 runs after its entry (F(7) = 13), never the 34 the first measure allowed; and each rule's offset is frozen at its entry: j is the rule's place among all rules ever entered in RULES.md's history (by the commit that first added it, then id), and the spread is the fixed 13, so neither adding nor removing a rule moves another rule's start. The step reports, for today's 30 rules, assuming every rule always holds and is confirmed whenever due, the largest number of rules due in any one run over the first 100 runs and the longest wait before any new rule's first check (checker-29 measured 9 and 13 for a 13-run spread); tests pin both numbers, pin that no rule waits more than 13 runs after its entry for its first check, and pin that adding a 35th rule changes no existing rule's start.

goal: A method to ASSEMBLE and REAPPLY context for the harness's own work, at the scope the owner chose on 2026-11-03 ('our working method first'). A fresh builder or checker, a new session, or the lead after a context compaction gets the same working context from RECORDS - tracked files and the harness's append-only ledgers, which may be uncommitted while a run is open - never from narrative memory or a transcript search; every assembled line names the record it came from, so it is re-verified when it is reapplied. A first draft of this method was opened in a ledger and withdrawn before any commit, after checker-29's plan review failed it with 11 findings; this run's first plan answered them and failed with 7 more, its second with 3 more, its third with 3 more, its fourth with 1 more; the sixth passed. This seventh plan amends only the stagger in SCHEDULE, by the lead's decision after checker-29 measured the adopted stagger's cost in step schedule (a never-confirmed rule could wait 34 runs, and adding a rule could move another's start). The owner named two structures: 'Eigenvectors and Fibonacci gears. Two structures.' EIGENVECTORS: the brief's CORE is the fixed point of reapplication - the standing rules in scope, verbatim, byte-identical every time they are assembled for the same scope (two different runs of one scope get the same CORE), unchanged by restating the inputs (entry order, line endings), never truncated - and the literal eigenvalue does its work in the schedule: Fibonacci intervals grow at the rate phi, the dominant eigenvalue of [[1,1],[1,0]] (eigenvector (phi, 1)), so a rule that keeps holding costs only logarithmically many re-checks. A spectral (eigenvector) ranking of rules is NOT built here: checker-29 showed on a 5-node example that power iteration on an acyclic citation graph reduces to plain counts, and a graph of source pointers is acyclic by construction, since a record can only name a record that existed before it; it is filed as a want, to be measured once checkers' confirmations give a co-confirmation matrix. FIBONACCI GEARS: each rule's re-verification interval steps through 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... runs in its scope; a checker's confirmation made while the rule is due advances it, a failure resets it to 1; an always-held rule confirmed whenever due is confirmed in its runs 1, 3, 6, 11, 19, ..., that is m times in its first F(m+3)-2 runs (8 times in 100). It lives in concordance-2 as a light tool on top of the harness; tools/harness.py, .claude/agents/* and every other grader are not edited. Nothing deploys to the box: the new files are accepted drift, named exactly, until the next concordance-2 deploy.

findings: tools/context.py _due's fallback does not do what its comment says, and a shallow clone silently breaks the frozen j. The comment reads 'out of the history git can show (a shallow clone): after all others', but in a shallow clone git log shows the boundary commit as a root that adds the whole of RULES.md, so every current rule is already in rule_ranks, the fallback catches nothing, and the ranks are computed from the truncated history. Measured with the step's own functions on a repository whose RULES.md went [c, a, b], then [a, c], then [a, aa, c], then [a, aa, c, z]: a full clone ranks a=1, b=2, c=3, aa=4, z=5 (starts a 9, aa 7, c 12, z 2); clones at --depth 1 and --depth 2 rank a=1, aa=2, c=3, z=4 (starts a 9, aa 4, c 12, z 7), with no rule caught by the fallback. So the same RULES.md at the same commit gives different first-due runs, DUE prints them with no warning, and the amended text's guarantee (j is the rule's place among all rules ever entered in RULES.md's history, so no rule moves another's start) fails, because rule b's removal moves aa and z. rule_entries has the same truncation: every entry becomes the boundary commit's time. It does not show today only because RULES.md has one commit. Fix: when git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository is true (the check fetch already makes), compute no schedule: print DUE as not computed, saying the clone cannot show RULES.md's history, or refuse the brief, and never print a start. Remove the fallback, or keep it only for git failing, with the same outcome and an honest comment. Test: a fixture with at least two RULES.md commits and a removal, cloned with --depth 1 through a file URL, asserting that no first-due run is printed.

findings: tools/context.py:949-951 (_rules_history: 'except (RecordsError, UnicodeError): continue  # ... history never changes, so every full clone skips it alike') can silently change a rank, so j is not frozen. History never changes, but the parser reading it does: a version is skipped by what today's parse_rules refuses. Measured with the step's own functions. (1) A skipped version hides the commit that first added a rule: RULES.md went [a, b], then [a, b, z] with stray prose inside an entry, then [a, b, z, y] fixed. The amended text ('by the commit that first added it, then id') gives z=3, y=4, starts z 12, y 7; the code gives y=3, z=4, starts z 7, y 12. (2) No bad version needed: RULES.md went [c, a, b], [a, c], [a, c, aa], ranking a=1, b=2, c=3, aa=4 (aa starts in run 7). A later commit adds a new required field to every entry and to parse_rules; every older version now fails to parse and is skipped, removed rule b is forgotten, and aa re-ranks to 2 (starts in run 4), with no warning, and rule_entries moves every entry to that commit too. So removing b does move another rule's start once the format changes, which the amended text rules out. Nothing tests old versions: the suite parses only the current RULES.md. Fix: the history walk needs only ids, so read them from each version's '## <id>' headings alone, independent of the field grammar and of whether the rest of the version parses; keep NoHistory for bytes that cannot be read. Tests: the two histories above, asserting z=3, y=4 and that a parser requiring a new field leaves every rank and entry unchanged.
